BCG’s 2026 survey of luxury shoppers finds that physical stores remain central to the category, but brands are undermining their advantage when customer knowledge disappears between visits, channels, and service interactions. The priority is not more automation; it is continuity that makes every encounter feel personally informed.

Recognition failures turn high-touch retail into a generic transactionAlthough luxury brands invest in personal service, 34% of returning clients feel treated as first-time customers. Those recognized rate the store experience far higher and are more likely to buy.

The relationship often breaks down after checkoutFragmented care and weak follow-up damage loyalty: 96% of customers say a poor post-sale experience would reduce future spending, while 43% receive no follow-up at all.

Luxury brands spend heavily to make customers feel special. Yet a BCG survey of luxury shoppers across North America, Europe, and Asia finds a striking disconnect: 34% of returning clients say they were treated like first-time customers. That failure has commercial consequences. Customers who are fully recognized rate their in-store experience 4.2 out of 5, versus 3.7 among those treated as new, and 46% say recognition makes them significantly more likely to purchase. (See “About the Study.”)

About the Study

BCG’s 2026 Experiential Luxury Survey explored how consumers experience luxury shopping before, during, and after a physical-store visit, as well as their attitudes toward the use of AI in the customer experience. The survey was completed in May 2026 by 669 respondents across North America, Europe, and Asia. Of those respondents, 436—65%—had purchased a luxury product or service in a physical store during the previous six months and qualified to complete the full survey.The qualified respondents represented a range of spending levels, from less than €5,000 to more than €300,000 annually on luxury goods and services. They shopped across categories, including fashion, travel, fine dining, beauty and wellness, jewelry, watches, and automobiles. The sample skewed younger and female: about 65% were women and 55% were ages 25 to 34.

The disconnect matters because the physical store still matters: 87% of luxury customers shop mostly in-store or split their shopping equally between stores and online channels. They continue to value the human experience—the chance to touch and feel products, engage with knowledgeable associates, and build an emotional connection with the brand. The question is no longer whether stores have a role, but whether brands give the people in them the information and tools to make every customer feel known every time the relationship resumes.That challenge is becoming more pressing as luxury itself changes. Wealth is shifting to a new generation, loyalty is becoming more conditional, AI is reshaping discovery, and purchase decisions increasingly extend beyond the individual buyer. Together, these shifts make continuity both harder to deliver and more valuable to achieve.BCG’s research points to four areas where that continuity breaks down: recognition and personalization, after-sales service, post-purchase follow-up, and the use of technology and AI. The failures look different, but they share one root cause: luxury brands too often lack the organizational memory to carry customer knowledge, context, and care from one interaction to the next.The Old Luxury Relationship Model Is Breaking
Luxury brands face a customer base that is broader, less loyal, and increasingly influenced by AI and social networks. (See Exhibit 1.)

Wealth is shifting to a new generation of affluent consumers whose expectations and behaviors differ from those that shaped traditional luxury relationship models. At the same time, loyalty is becoming more conditional. Even highly valuable customers spread their attention and spending across multiple brands, increasing the premium on recognition, relevance, and a trusted human relationship.The journey is changing as well. AI is becoming an important gateway to discovery and consideration, altering how consumers search, compare, and decide. Luxury purchases are also increasingly shaped by family members, peers, and creators—not just the individual buyer.These shifts expose the limits of relationship models built around individual transactions, channels, and customers. Many luxury brands are asking associates to deliver relationship-based service with transaction-based infrastructure. Training and coaching remain essential in a category built on human interaction, but they cannot compensate for fragmented information and disconnected systems.The survey shows where that strain appears. Customers rate core store interactions strongly, but ratings fall at touchpoints that depend more heavily on the brand retaining and applying customer context over time. (See Exhibit 2.) The weakness lies less in what associates can deliver in the moment than in what the brand enables them to remember from one interaction to the next.

Where Luxury Loses the Relationship
The continuity problem surfaces in different ways across the customer journey. A returning customer may go unrecognized, the relationship may fade after the sale, or technology may add friction rather than remove it. In each case, the underlying problem is the same: customer knowledge and context fail to travel with the customer. (See Exhibit 3.)

Recognition and personalization: Customers should not need to reintroduce themselves. The problem is not simply whether an associate remembers a face or name. In our survey, 30% of customers say their profile with the brand does not carry from one location to another. That failure of portability forces customers to reestablish preferences, purchase history, and relationship context that the brand should already know. Personalization works only if that information is available when and where an associate needs it.After-sales service: Luxury should not end at the checkout. Fragmentation after the sale can do lasting commercial damage. The consequences are substantial: 96% of customers say a poor experience would reduce their loyalty, spending, or future purchases. Yet customers seeking care, repairs, or support can still find themselves chasing information, repeating details, and navigating disconnected service functions. In a category built on long-term relationships, the quality of ownership matters as much as the quality of the transaction.Post-purchase follow-up: Silence is a relationship failure. The relationship can weaken even when nothing has gone wrong. Among surveyed customers, 43% received no follow-up at all after their purchase. Post-purchase engagement is distinct from after-sales service: it is the brand’s opportunity to remain relevant through thoughtful outreach, recognition, and continued attention. Customers’ own descriptions of feeling valued reinforce the point: being remembered and receiving proactive follow-up matter well beyond the moment of purchase.Technology and AI: Make the associate smarter, not scarcer. Luxury customers are not resistant to technology, but they are selective about its role. Seventy-nine percent say replacing human interaction with automation would detract from the luxury experience. Technology adds value when it removes friction, connects customer history, anticipates needs, and helps associates deliver a more informed interaction. The winning use of AI in luxury may be almost invisible to the customer: technology working behind the scenes to make the human interaction more informed, seamless, and personal.Make Every Interaction Pick Up Where the Last One Ended
The management challenge is to turn these separate moments into one continuous relationship. The target state is simple: every interaction should pick up where the last one ended. That means organizing the customer experience around the relationship, not around separate channels, systems, and functions. It requires a unified customer profile, shared visibility into inventory and service, and a continuous record that associates and teams can use across the journey.Keep the store at the center of the relationship. Digital adoption is not a reason to pull investments away from the physical experience. For many luxury customers, the store remains where reassurance, human connection, and emotional engagement are strongest. Brands should double down on what makes that experience irreplaceable: associate quality, environment, and the felt sense of being genuinely known.Make the customer profile portable. The first infrastructure priority is fundamental: customer knowledge must be available wherever the relationship resumes. A returning customer should not have to reconstruct preferences, purchase history, service issues, or relevant household relationships because an interaction moves from online to store, from one location to another, or from one associate to the next.Customers rank a portable profile across stores and online as the highest-priority AI-enabled investment in BCG’s survey. The value is not the profile itself but what it enables: associates can prepare for a visit, recognize the customer, understand prior purchases and preferences, and continue the relationship without forcing the customer to start over. Brands should consider tracking recognition as a formal business metric alongside conversion and satisfaction.Extend the relationship beyond the transaction. The sale should deepen the relationship, not end it. Brands should link service history, repair status, product-care needs, prior conversations, and follow-up to the customer record.Start with what customers rank highest: complimentary cleaning and maintenance at regular intervals, a dedicated care concierge, and real-time digital visibility into repair status. Give the customer a clear relationship owner across their after-sales care rather than forcing them to navigate disconnected service functions.With that foundation, after-sales care can become proactive. Brands can anticipate maintenance needs, provide timely service updates, and tailor follow-ups to what the customer owns and how the relationship has developed. The goal is not simply better service when a problem occurs. It is to make ownership itself part of the luxury experience.Put AI in service of the associate. AI can make this architecture more powerful, but its role is to strengthen the human interaction, not displace it. Before a visit, it can surface previous purchases, preferences, occasions, and household context. During the interaction, it can provide complete customer history and real-time inventory. Afterward, it can support personalized follow-up, care and service updates, invitations, curated recommendations, and predictive care alerts.Associates still need the judgment, empathy, and relationship skills that define luxury service. AI should give them better context, not replace those capabilities.The broader shift is from investing in isolated channels and point solutions to connecting customer data, inventory, service, and associate context across the journey. Much of the required technology already exists. The management challenge is to connect and govern it so every interaction begins with what the brand already knows and strengthens the human relationship rather than interrupting it.The Relationship Is the Advantage
In luxury, making customers feel known has always been part of the relationship. What is changing is the infrastructure required to deliver that feeling consistently. As customers move across stores, channels, households, and service moments, the brands that stand out will be those that give the entire organization the memory to make that feeling travel—and put it in the hands of people who know how to use it.The advantage lies in making recognition, care, and continuity feel effortless even when the systems behind them are complex. Technology can enable that experience, but the value is ultimately human: a customer who feels remembered, understood, and worth knowing over time. The store isn’t the problem luxury brands need to solve. The relationship is.
